findings.summary: Open Sound Control (OSC) is a networking protocol for connecting sound synthesizers, computers, and multimedia devices, originally intended for sharing music performance data such as note sequences and parameters. It serves as an alternative to MIDI when higher resolution and a richer parameter space are desired. OSC messages are transported over UDP/IP and Ethernet, or over USB wrapped in SLIP. The protocol uses hierarchical address patterns resembling file paths, type tag strings to denote argument types, and binary-encoded arguments. Messages may be grouped into nested bundles with timestamps to schedule future delivery. OSC's advantages include internet connectivity, data type resolution, and symbolic path specification, though it requires more bandwidth than MIDI and lacks standardized messages across devices.

mechanisms.title: Address patterns and type tags
mechanisms.explanation: OSC messages are structured with a hierarchical address pattern (e.g., /oscillator/4/frequency) and a type tag string (e.g., ,fi) that compactly represents argument types. The address patterns form a namespace similar to a file system, while type tags denote binary-encoded arguments such as 32-bit integers or IEEE floating point numbers.

mechanisms.title: Bundles with timestamps
mechanisms.explanation: OSC messages may be combined into bundles, which themselves may be nested. Each bundle contains a timestamp that determines whether the server should respond immediately or at a scheduled future time, allowing coordinated delivery of multiple messages.

unknowns: No standardized messages across different devices
No defined namespace for common musical exchanges such as sending Middle C
Each participating server must know what messages it can send; the standard does not provide programmatic discovery
The specification does not define any particular OSC Methods or Containers; all messages are implementation-defined and vary server to server
